Welcome toEngine Meets Heat Pump

A claimed engine drives a reversible one backwards — how good can it really be?

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

About: a claimed engine X coupled to a reversible engine R

Source

Concept
Carnot's theorem (Fermi Notes, §2.3, Fig. 12): a claimed engine X, known only by its efficiency ηX, is coupled to a reversible engine R working between the same reservoirs at Th and Tc, one of the pair running backwards as a heat pump.
Serves
Explaining, from the energy bookkeeping of one cycle of the coupled pair, what limits the efficiency of any engine between two reservoirs, and what that means for reversible engines between them.
Inquiry
Six questions: read one cycle's net result, identify the law it bears on, lower the claim until the net result vanishes, try a lower claim, swap which engine drives which, and change the reservoir temperatures. A closing card states Carnot's theorem.
Misconception
Each wrong choice carries a common misconception, and its feedback answers that misconception directly. Nothing on screen labels a net result as allowed or forbidden, so each one is judged from the bars.
On screen
X's efficiency is a claim under test, and the coupled pair is a thought experiment. Grey boxes are the hot and cold reservoirs; circles are X and R, each labelled engine or heat pump by its running direction. Heat arrows are drawn in the canvas ink colour (black on the light theme, near-white on the dark theme), work arrows in blue; every width is proportional to its energy (one fixed scale per window size, 40 to 56 px per 1000 J, never under 2 px) and every arrow is labelled in joules. The two are sized so each exchanges 1000 J with the hot reservoir per cycle. Dots drift along the arrows at one fixed, slow speed only to show the direction of flow; ▶ Play animates nothing else, since every energy shown is per cycle.
Measured
The band below the diagram sums one cycle of the pair: heat gained by each reservoir and work leaving the assembly, each bar labelled in joules, on a fixed axis from −400 J to +400 J (a bar beyond it is marked off-scale). The Readouts panel gives the same totals to the nearest joule, with ηX, the work X and R each do or use, and, from question 4, R's efficiency; a negative work total means work supplied from outside.
Controls
A checkbox shows or hides the net-result bars (a view option; it changes no physics). ηX: X's claimed efficiency, 0.05 to 0.90. Th: 500 K to 800 K. Tc: 200 K to 400 K. Arrangement: X drives R backwards, or R drives X backwards with X taken to be reversible.

Pedagogy principles applied

PrincipleHow this sim honours it
Commit, then checkEach of the six questions is a gated choice; the arrows, bars and Readouts panel are the evidence it is checked against.
No verdict on screenNo warning, colour change or mark appears for any net result, and R's efficiency joins the Readouts only with question 4, after the student has found the claim at which the totals vanish.
Operational quantitiesEvery arrow carries its energy in joules and a width proportional to it; one-cycle totals are read off the bars and the readout line.
Stable scalesArrow widths and the −400 J to +400 J bar axis never rescale, so a change of control shows as a change of size.
What stays fixedThe heat each of X and R exchanges with the hot reservoir stays at 1000 J per cycle at every setting and in both arrangements.
The claim as a black boxX is a bare circle with no working substance or cycle drawn inside; it enters only through the number ηX.
Honest roundingEvery label, bar and readout is rounded from shared whole-joule values, so the bookkeeping on screen always closes.

Guided Inquiry

1 · One cycle of the pair

Keep Th = 500 K, Tc = 300 K, ηX = 0.50 and the arrangement in which X drives R backwards. Read the labels on the arrows, the Net result bars and the Readouts panel. What has one cycle of the pair done to the world outside it?

2 · Which law is broken

Stay at the same setting. Which law of thermodynamics does this net result break?

3 · Lowering the claimed efficiency

Keep Th = 500 K and Tc = 300 K, and lower ηX slowly from 0.50, watching the bars. At what claimed efficiency does the net result of a cycle become nothing at all?

4 · A less efficient engine

R's efficiency, ηR = 1 − Tc/Th, now appears in the Readouts panel.

Keep Th = 500 K and Tc = 300 K, and set ηX = 0.30. What is the net result of a cycle now, and is it forbidden?

5 · Reversing the arrangement

Keep Th = 500 K, Tc = 300 K and ηX = 0.30, and switch to the arrangement in which R drives X backwards, with X taken to be reversible. What does the pair do now?

6 · The highest possible claim

Set Th = 800 K and Tc = 200 K and use the first arrangement. X's makers say it uses a new working substance far better than an ideal gas. What is the highest efficiency they can claim without the pair turning heat from the cold reservoir alone into work?

7 · What the pair has shown

No engine beats a reversible one. If any engine X between two reservoirs were more efficient than the reversible engine R, driving R backwards with it would turn heat from a single reservoir wholly into work, which the Kelvin statement forbids (questions 1–4).

All reversible engines are equally efficient. If X is itself reversible, running the pair the other way shows it cannot be less efficient than R either (question 5).

Together these are Carnot's theorem: every reversible engine between Th and Tc has the efficiency of the Carnot cycle, η = 1 − Tc/Th, and no engine can do better, whatever its working substance (question 6).

The Physics

Carnot’s Theorem: Engine Meets Heat Pump · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A claimed engine X is coupled to a reversible engine R working between the same two reservoirs, one of the pair running backwards as a heat pump. The sim keeps the energy books for one cycle of the pair, and reading those books is how the notes prove Carnot’s theorem.

What you'll learn

  • How the heat and work of one cycle of the pair add up.
  • How the net result of that cycle depends on ηX, Th and Tc.
  • Which statement of the second law the net result bears on.
  • How the account changes when the roles of X and R are swapped.
  • How X’s working substance enters the argument.
The apparatus (notes, Figure 12), sized so that X and R each exchange Qh with the hot reservoir.

What's on screen

  • Grey boxes: the hot reservoir at Th (top) and the cold reservoir at Tc (bottom).
  • Circles X and R, each named engine or heat pump by the way it runs.
  • Dark arrows are heat, blue arrows are work. Each width follows its energy, and each carries its value in joules.
  • Dots drifting along the arrows show only the direction of flow.
  • Bars (below): the net result of one cycle outside the pair, on a fixed −400 J to +400 J axis.
  • Readouts: the same totals to the nearest joule, and what is inside the pair.
See itStart the pair running again at your current settings. Watch for: the dots drifting along the arrows while the arrow widths, their labels and the bars stay as they are.

03

One cycle of the pair leaves a net result

X is known only by ηX. As an engine it takes Qh from the hot reservoir, does work WX = ηXQh and rejects Qc = (1 − ηX)Qh to the cold one. R is reversible with efficiency ηR = 1 − Tc/Th. Driven by X it runs as a heat pump: it takes in WR = ηRQh, draws Q′c = (1 − ηR)Qh from the cold reservoir and delivers Qh to the hot one.

The pair is sized so that R delivers exactly the Qh that X draws, so the hot reservoir ends the cycle unchanged. Of X’s work, WR goes to R and the surplus leaves the assembly:

Notes, p. 44. Positive W is work leaving the assembly.

The cold reservoir gains Qc from X and loses Q′c to R, so it changes by

The cold reservoir loses exactly the work that leaves.
See itRun the pair at your current settings and read the three bars. Watch for: the cold bar and the work bar equal in size and opposite in sign, with the hot bar at 0 J.
04

That result breaks the Kelvin statement

Take ηX > ηR, so that W is positive, and test the result against the second law.

The first law holds: the work that leaves equals the heat the cold reservoir lost, so energy balances. The Clausius statement forbids heat passing from a colder body to a hotter one as the sole result. The hot reservoir is unchanged, so nothing has been delivered up to it.

The Kelvin statement forbids the complete conversion of heat drawn from a single reservoir into work as the sole result. That is what the pair has done: the cold reservoir lost heat, an equal amount of work left, and nothing else changed, because X and R are back where they started after each cycle.

Such a pair cannot exist, so no engine X can have ηX > ηR. Hence ηX ≤ ηR (notes, p. 44).

See itRaise the claim well above R’s efficiency, in the first arrangement. Watch for: the work bar above zero, the cold bar below zero by the same amount, and the hot bar still at 0 J.
05

A claim below ηR breaks no law

If ηX < ηR, then W is negative. Work has to be supplied from outside, and the cold reservoir gains the same amount of heat, because X rejects more heat there than R draws. The pair has turned work into heat. The Kelvin statement concerns heat becoming work, so it says nothing against this: X is simply a poorer engine than R.

At ηX = ηR all three bars read 0 J. The slider moves in steps of 0.01, so it can land on ηR exactly only when ηR is a multiple of 0.01, as it is at 500 K and 300 K.

W = (ηX − ηR)Qh with Qh = 1000 J, for Th = 500 K and Tc = 300 K, X driving R. The dot is the opening claim.
See itLower the claim below R’s efficiency, in the first arrangement. Watch for: the work bar below zero, the cold bar above zero by the same amount, and the hot bar still at 0 J.
06

Swapping the roles rules out a weaker reversible X

So far X could be any engine. Now take X to be reversible as well, so that it can also be run backwards. R can then drive X, as in the second arrangement. R does WR = ηRQh, and X, as a heat pump, needs only WX = ηXQh to return Qh to the hot reservoir. The surplus is W = (ηR − ηX)Qh. If ηX < ηR it is positive and comes from the cold reservoir alone: the same forbidden result.

The first arrangement rules out ηX > ηR, and the second rules out ηX < ηR. A reversible X is left with ηX = ηR. Every reversible engine between the same two reservoirs has the same efficiency, whatever it is made of, and the ideal-gas Carnot cycle gives its value:

Notes, (2.31).
See itSwap to the second arrangement with a claim below R’s efficiency. Watch for: work leaving again, drawn from the cold reservoir alone, although X is now the weaker engine.
07

The ceiling does not depend on the working substance

The bookkeeping never looks inside X. Its working substance, its cycle and its size do not appear in W: only ηX, ηR and Qh do. So whatever X is made of, a claim above 1 − Tc/Th would let the pair turn heat from the cold reservoir alone into work, and no engine between these two reservoirs can have a higher efficiency.

At Th = 800 K and Tc = 200 K the ceiling is 0.75. A claim of 0.75 balances the books exactly; a claim of 0.90 leaves 150 J of cold-reservoir heat turned into work each cycle. A better substance than an ideal gas does not move the ceiling.

The ceiling depends on the two temperatures alone. It rises when Th rises or Tc falls. A real engine falls below it.

See itSet Th = 800 K and Tc = 200 K, with the claim at 0.75. Watch for: all three bars at 0 J.
See itRaise the claim to 0.90 at the same temperatures. Watch for: a work bar of +150 J and a cold bar of −150 J, with the hot bar still at 0 J.
08

Where it matters

  • Power stations. Whatever the fuel or the design, a plant working between Th and Tc cannot exceed 1 − Tc/Th. Steam near 800 K with condensers near 300 K gives a ceiling of 0.625, and real plants fall short of it. The notes mention a coastal station whose condensers are cooled by the sea, which keeps Tc low.
  • Judging a claim. An engine said to beat 1 − Tc/Th between its two temperatures can be rejected without opening it, by this argument alone.
  • Heat pumps and refrigerators. R in the sim runs as a heat pump. The same argument, run the other way, shows that no heat pump delivers more heat per unit of work than a reversible one between the same temperatures.
09

Summary

In one line. Carnot’s theorem is proved by bookkeeping: couple a claimed engine to a reversible one and read what one cycle of the pair does to the world outside.

Key points

  • With both exchanging Qh at the hot reservoir, the surplus work is W = (ηX − ηR)Qh, drawn entirely from the cold reservoir.
  • ηX > ηR would violate the Kelvin statement, so no engine beats a reversible one.
  • All reversible engines between two reservoirs share ηR = 1 − Tc/Th.

Common mix-ups

  • “R, run backwards, undoes X, so nothing happens.” R returns Qh to the hot reservoir, but the cold reservoir still changes unless ηX = ηR.
  • “The surplus work breaks the first law.” The work equals the heat the cold reservoir lost, so energy balances. The Kelvin statement is what forbids it.

Things to try on your own

  • Set Th = 700 K and Tc = 350 K. Work out ηR, set ηX to it, and check that all three bars read 0 J.
  • At ηX = 0.60, Th = 500 K and Tc = 300 K, compare the work bar in the two arrangements and note which one shows work leaving.
